implementation_notes: The standard library emulates immutability for ordinary classes: @dataclass(frozen=True) installs __setattr__ and __delattr__ that raise FrozenInstanceError, so an instance cannot be rebound, and frozen also enables __hash__ when every field is hashable. The emulation is explicitly shallow and escapable - object.__setattr__ reaches around the guard, and a list, dict or set field is still mutated in place through any reference - so fields should hold immutable values (tuple, frozenset, another frozen dataclass) and updates should go through dataclasses.replace. The hand-written form is still needed when a class must be mutable internally but expose an immutable face. For computed fields in __post_init__, use object.__setattr__(self, 'field', value) since direct assignment raises FrozenInstanceError even inside __post_init__. For deep copies in updates, combine replace() with copy.deepcopy() or use persistent collections instead.
pitfalls: frozen=True is shallow: list, dict and set fields can still be mutated in place, and a field holding a mutable object makes the instance unhashable in practice (hash() raises TypeError).
object.__setattr__(obj, name, value) bypasses the generated guard completely; frozen is a contract, not a capability.
A frozen dataclass can only be subclassed by another frozen dataclass, and mutable defaults must still go through field(default_factory=...).

dataclasses.replace() is a shallow copy: nested mutable objects are shared between the old and new instance. A frozen dataclass with a list field where one caller appends corrupts the state visible to all other holders of old instances.
Assigning to self in __post_init__ of a frozen dataclass raises FrozenInstanceError: must use object.__setattr__(self, 'field', value) inside __post_init__ only.
object.__setattr__(obj, name, value) bypasses the generated guard completely, and so does direct __dict__ manipulation; frozen is a contract, not a capability.

dataclasses.replace() is a shallow copy: nested mutable objects are shared between the old and new instance. Using replace() on a frozen dataclass with a list field means both instances reference the same list, which can corrupt state if one caller appends.

Assigning to self in __post_init__ of a frozen dataclass raises FrozenInstanceError: you must use object.__setattr__(self, 'field_name', value) inside __post_init__ only; this is the officially documented escape hatch.

attrs frozen=True on slotted classes has a minor per-init performance overhead compared to unfrozen slotted classes; for very hot paths creating millions of instances, prefer frozen dict classes (non-slotted) or profile first.

pydantic ConfigDict(frozen=True) on a model with a dict field: model.a = 'x' raises ValidationError but model.dict_field['key'] = 'val' succeeds silently; immutability is at the attribute level only, not deep.
MappingProxyType({}) is not hashable and can be mutated via gc.get_referents() in CPython; prefer a frozendict approach (PEP 818) or immutables.Map for truly hashable immutable dicts.

Shallow copying nested mutable objects: List.copyOf() and tuple() both copy the container but not the elements; if contained elements are mutable, holders of element references can mutate the logical state of the supposedly immutable parent.

variants.name: typing.NamedTuple with _replace
variants.implementation_notes: typing.NamedTuple (or collections.namedtuple) builds a tuple subclass, so the instance is genuinely immutable by Python's tuple semantics, hashable, comparable by value and accepted anywhere a tuple is expected. _replace returns a new instance with changed fields. This is the cheapest immutable record in the language and interoperates with tuple unpacking, but it cannot hide the tuple protocol and offers no state beyond the declared fields. NamedTuple cannot have methods with private state (no __slots__ either), and field defaults must be simple values. Choose NamedTuple over frozen dataclass when you need genuine tuple immutability without any escape hatch, or when interoperability with tuple-unpacking APIs is important. Choose frozen dataclass when you need methods, custom __init__ behaviour, or integration with dataclasses.replace().
variants.code_sketch:
from typing import NamedTuple

class Point(NamedTuple):
    x: float
    y: float
    label: str = "origin"

p = Point(1.0, 2.0)
q = p._replace(x=10.0)      # p is unchanged; q.x == 10.0
pitfalls: The tuple guarantee is only as deep as the elements: a NamedTuple holding a list is mutable through that list and becomes unhashable.
Field names must not start with an underscore and defaults must be simple values, so sentinel-style or private-field APIs are awkward.
_replace and _fields are namedtuple-specific: code that treats the value as a plain tuple (or serialises it) silently loses the names.
NamedTuple cannot define __slots__; each instance carries a full __dict__, making it memory-inefficient for millions of small records compared to frozen slotted dataclasses.

variants.name: attrs @frozen with validators and converters
variants.implementation_notes: attrs provides @define (or @attr.s) and @frozen (equivalent to define(frozen=True)) as an alternative to dataclasses. attrs frozen classes install a custom __setattr__ that raises FrozenInstanceError, and support field-level validators, converters, and factory functions. attrs uses slotted classes by default (Python 3.10+ slots=True is the default), which gives better memory efficiency and faster attribute access than dataclasses. The frozen slotted implementation uses (an aggressively cached) object.__setattr__() to set attributes during __init__, which has a minor performance cost per instantiation. For very high-frequency instantiation, frozen dict classes (slots=False) have negligible overhead. attrs also supports on_setattr hooks with attrs.setters.frozen for per-attribute immutability and provides hash code caching via cache_hash=True on frozen classes.
pitfalls: attrs frozen=True on slotted classes has a minor per-init performance cost vs unfrozen slotted classes due to the cached object.__setattr__ path; profile before assuming it is a bottleneck.
object.__setattr__(self, name, value) still bypasses the frozen guard inside __init__ or __attrs_post_init__; attrs uses this internally to set fields, so it cannot be blocked without breaking init.
A frozen attrs class cannot define its own __setattr__; this is a documented limitation of the frozen parameter.
cache_hash=True on frozen attrs classes caches the hash value in __hash__, which is safe only when the instance is truly immutable; mutating the object after hashing invalidates the cache.
Subclasses of a frozen attrs class are also frozen automatically; this is inherited but can be surprising.

variants.name: Persistent collections (pypersistent, pyrsistent, immutables)
variants.idiom_name: pypersistent / pyrsistent / immutables persistent data structures
variants.implementation_notes: For immutable objects with large nested structures that are updated frequently, copying the whole graph with dataclasses.replace() or copy.deepcopy() is O(n). Persistent data structures (pypersistent, pyrsistent, immutables) use Hash Array Mapped Tries (HAMT) to share unchanged structure between versions, making each update O(log n) regardless of size. pypersistent (C++ HAMT) provides PersistentDict, PersistentList, PersistentSet, PersistentArrayMap, PersistentSortedDict; pyrsistent (pure Python) provides PVector, PMap, PSet, PRecord, PClass with evolvers for batched mutable construction before freezing. immutables.Map is a HAMT-backed dict used internally by CPython contextvars. These are appropriate when: the structure is large and frequently updated, you need undo/redo or version snapshots, or you need thread-safe shared state without locks. Choose pypersistent for maximum performance, pyrsistent for a pure-Python fallback with more features, and immutables.Map when you specifically need a Map with dict interoperability.
pitfalls: Persistent collections have O(log n) lookup cost (HAMT depth), which is essentially O(1) for up to millions of entries but may be slower than a flat dict for small, frequently accessed structures.

The immutability of a persistent collection is shallow: if a PersistentDict contains a list as a value, that list is still mutable. Use nested persistent collections or freeze values for deep immutability.
pypersistent requires C++ build tooling; it is not a pure-Python wheel. On platforms without a C++ compiler, fall back to pyrsistent.

Structural sharing means that two PersistentDicts with different histories may share internal nodes; this is safe but means that mutating through one reference to a shared sub-structure affects what both dicts appear to hold at that sub-structure (if the sub-structure itself is mutable).

evolver pattern (pyrsistent): calling .evolve() on an evolver mutates the evolver's view, not the original; calling .persistent() finalises and returns a new immutable persistent collection. Forgetting to call .persistent() leaks mutable state.
